latin.81: IV. Veniamus igitur ad verf. 17. Ex eo simile, inquit D. G. argumentum emergit. Cuius delicto & lapsu mors semper regnavit & regnatura est in finem seculi, eius delicti poena pervadit in omnes. Mors enim certe ab Apostolo ponitur, tanquam causae illius effectum. At uno Adami delicto mors hactenus in omnes regnavit, & porro regnatura est usque ad finem seculi. Igitur delicti & lapsus illius Adae poena in omnes pervagatur.
latin.82: Concedo totum arg. Quis enim nostrum unquam negavit, lapsus Adae poenam in omnes esse pervagatam? Tantum contendimus, inter eam & lapsum Adae intervenisse vitium originale cui proxime poena debetur.
latin.83: Est igitur lapsus Adae prima causa regni mortis, sed proxima est ab illo productum peccatum omnibus inhaerens, quod quia regnat, etiam mors regnat. Certe peccatum quod in hominibus non modo est, sed vivit; non modo vivit sed regnat; cui serviunt, cui obediunt, cujus lex est in membris. Id non est peccatum actuale Adami, sed hujus effectum, corruptio inhaerens.
latin.84: V. Ex verf. 18. simili ratione ac supra colligit. Per cuius delictum condemnatio in omnes homines venit, propter illius delictum poena irrogatur omnibus: Atqui per unius Adae delictum condemnatio venit in omnes. Ergo propter unius Adae delictum, poena irrogatur omnibus ejus posteris. Primum negari potest major propositio. aliud enim est per aliquem esse aliquid, aliud propter aliquem; per calamum scribo, non tamen propter calamum; per judicem est condemnatio, non tamen propter judicem.
latin.85: Deinde distinguo propter ut supra. Nam vel causam remotam designat, vel proximam. Si illam, conceditur totum argumentum; si hanc, negatur propositio. Est enim, ut multoties inculcavi, primum Adami peccatum actuale causa nostri peccati inhaerentis, & hoc causa mortis: quod autem est causa causae, id causa est etiam effectus. Aut cum Pelagio, Pighio, & Socino negandum est peccatum inhaerens ejusque reatus, aut impossibile est ex verbis Apostoli imputationem peccati Adae actualis antecedentem seu immediatam efficere.

pass_a.81: Placeus opens the next head: so we come to verse 17. Garissoles (D. G.) claims that from this verse an argument like the earlier ones rises. The major runs: whoever is such that by his offense and fall death has always reigned and will reign to the age's end — that person's offense brings a penalty that spreads through everyone. Support: the Apostle treats death as the effect of that cause. The minor: by Adam's one offense death has already reigned over everyone up to now, and will keep reigning through to the age's end. Conclusion Garissoles wants: therefore the penalty of Adam's offense and fall spreads through everyone.
pass_a.82: Placeus answers by granting the whole of that argument as stated. Rhetorical challenge: who among us has ever denied that Adam's fall's penalty has spread through everyone? The real dispute is narrower: between the penalty and Adam's fall there stands intervening original vice, and the penalty is owed to that vice as its proximate debtor.
pass_a.83: Therefore Adam's fall is death's reign's first cause, while the proximate cause is the sin that fall produced and that now inheres in everyone. Because that inhering sin reigns, death reigns too. Placeus presses the description: the sin in people not merely exists but lives; not merely lives but reigns; people serve it, obey it, and carry its law in their members. That reigning thing is not Adam's own actual sin; it is the effect of Adam's actual sin — namely inhering corruption. This closes the reply to the verse-17 argument.
pass_a.84: Next head: from verse 18 Garissoles gathers by the same pattern used above. Major: if through someone's offense condemnation came on all humans, then on account of that someone's offense a penalty is laid on everyone. Minor: through the one Adam's offense condemnation did come on everyone. Conclusion: therefore on account of the one Adam's offense a penalty is laid on all his descendants. Placeus's first cut: the major can be refused. Being through someone is not the same as being on account of someone. Illustrations: writing happens through a pen, not on account of the pen; condemnation happens through a judge, not on account of the judge.
pass_a.85: Second cut: Placeus distinguishes the phrase "on account of" the same way he did earlier. It can name a remote cause or a proximate cause. If remote, he grants Garissoles the whole argument; if proximate, he refuses the premise. Reason repeated often: Adam's first actual sin causes our inhering sin, and our inhering sin causes death; whatever causes a cause also causes that cause's effect. Hinge: either join Pelagius, Pighius, and Socinus in denying inhering sin and its guilt, or you cannot squeeze out of the Apostle's wording an antecedent / immediate imputation of Adam's actual sin. Stops before the verse-19 head.

81: IV. Let us come, then, to verse 17. From it, says D. Garissoles, a similar argument arises. The one by whose offense and fall death has always reigned and will reign to the end of the age — that one's offense-penalty pervades all. For death is certainly set by the Apostle as the effect of that cause (Romans 5:17). But by one offense of Adam death has so far reigned over all, and will go on reigning to the end of the age. Therefore the penalty of that offense and fall of Adam pervades all.
82: I grant the whole argument. Which of us ever denied that the penalty of Adam's fall has pervaded all? We contend only this: between that penalty and Adam's fall, original vice has intervened, and to that vice the penalty is owed proximately.
83: So Adam's fall is the first cause of death's reign, but the proximate cause is the sin produced from it and inhering in all; and because that sin reigns, death also reigns. Certainly the sin in human beings not only is, but lives; not only lives but reigns — the sin they serve, the sin they obey, whose law is in their members. That is not Adam's actual sin, but its effect: inhering corruption.
84: V. From verse 18 he gathers by a similar reason as above. The one through whose offense condemnation came upon all human beings — on account of that one's offense a penalty is inflicted on all. But through one Adam's offense condemnation came upon all. Therefore on account of one Adam's offense a penalty is inflicted on all his posterity (Romans 5:18). First, the major premise can be denied. For it is one thing for something to be through someone, another for it to be on account of someone: I write with a pen, yet not on account of the pen; condemnation is through a judge, yet not on account of the judge.
85: Next I distinguish "on account of" as above. It marks either a remote cause or a proximate one. If the remote, the whole argument is granted; if the proximate, the premise is denied. For, as I have driven home many times, Adam's first actual sin is the cause of our inhering sin, and this is the cause of death; and what is the cause of a cause is also the cause of the effect. Either, with Pelagius, Pighius, and Socinus, inhering sin and its guilt must be denied, or it is impossible from the Apostle's words to force an antecedent or immediate imputation of Adam's actual sin.
